docs.title: Welcome to Chromaticity Help
docs.text:
This is the in-app help corpus shipped inside the Chromaticity desktop runtime. Pages here are authored clean-room from chromaticity's own ADRs and development standards — none of this content derives from any reference application's embedded documentation.

The Wave 1d-α PR 1 scaffold establishes the rails:

  • A mkdocs source tree under docs-corpus/docs/.
  • A static-HTML build emitted to dist/help/ and bundled into the Tauri binary via app/shell/tauri.conf.json bundle.resources.
  • A Help view (src/lib/views/Help.svelte) that surfaces the bundled HTML pages through Tauri's convertFileSrc resource path.

Future waves author the real corpus content: scene-format reference, operator hotkey catalog, MIDI / OSC routing, troubleshooting guides, and onboarding walkthroughs. The two pages shipped in PR 1 (this page and About) are placeholders that validate the routing + build pipeline end-to-end.

docs.title: About this Help corpus
docs.text: The Chromaticity Help corpus is a static documentation site built with MkDocs using the Material theme. The corpus is authored under docs-corpus/docs/ in the chromaticity source tree, built locally with mkdocs build, and emitted to dist/help/ for inclusion in the desktop application bundle.

docs.title: Authoring posture
docs.text: All Help corpus content is original chromaticity prose. Per the clean-room policy (docs/29-cleanroom-legal-policy-baseline.md), no text, structure, or per-page taxonomy is derived from any reference application's embedded documentation. Authors who land corpus content attest to clean-room provenance in the PR body.

docs.title: Build chain
docs.text:
The mkdocs build step runs locally before cargo tauri build so that the static HTML output exists at link time and is bundled into the desktop binary. CI does not currently run mkdocs build; that integration is Wave 1d-β release-eng scope.

This is the second placeholder page that exists to validate routing between corpus pages. Future waves replace this content with a real About / Version / Changelog page.

docs.title: Audio Reactivity
docs.text: Chromaticity is an audio-reactive runtime: every scene can sample tempo, energy, and per-band spectrum data from the live audio input and bind them as GLSL uniforms. This page describes how audio enters the engine, how the analysis pipeline produces uniform snapshots, and how the operator HUD widgets and the GLSL shader binding layer consume that data.

docs.title: Audio path overview
docs.text:
The audio pipeline runs across three thread boundaries, established by the runtime thread-and-process model:

  1. Audio input — Operating-system audio capture is owned by the audio analysis thread. A frame-source implementation pulls interleaved sample data, mixes multi-channel input down to mono, and produces a fixed-shape AudioFrame value type.
  2. Analysis — The same thread calls extract_uniform_snapshot on each frame. The function is pure: same input frame yields the same output snapshot. Its responsibilities are RMS, peak, an eight-band log-spaced FFT, and a single-frame autocorrelation BPM estimate.
  3. Hand-off — The producer-side runtime publishes the snapshot into a shared Arc<Mutex<AudioUniformSnapshot>> cell. The scheduler tick reads the cell, marshals it to GPU uniform inputs for the render path, and emits it to the UI over the engine-to-UI IPC bridge.

The audio crate intentionally does not depend on the render or IPC crates; consumers marshal the plain-data snapshot into whatever surface they own. This is what lets the analysis thread stay render-agnostic and lets the IPC bridge attach without any audio-side churn.

docs.title: What the snapshot carries
docs.text:
Each tick publishes the following fields:

Field Range Notes bpm [50, 220] Estimated tempo, clamped to the musical range; defaults to 120 on too-short frames rms [0, 1] Root-mean-square energy of the mono-mixed frame, clamped at 1 for out-of-range PCM input peak [0, 1] Peak absolute magnitude of the mono-mixed frame fft_bands[8] [0, 1] per band Eight log-spaced FFT magnitudes covering 20 Hz to 20 kHz

The snapshot is a #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)] value type; consumers can copy it freely without coordination. The default shape is the all-zero baseline that consumers see during the no-audio-yet startup window.

docs.title: The eight-to-four band reduction
docs.text:
The slice-1 producer publishes eight log-spaced FFT bands. Several operator-facing widgets expose four named bands ("bass", "low-mid", "mid", "high") to keep the UX legible. The reduction combines adjacent bands pairwise:

  • bass = (fft[0] + fft[1]) / 2
  • low-mid = (fft[2] + fft[3]) / 2
  • mid = (fft[4] + fft[5]) / 2
  • high = (fft[6] + fft[7]) / 2

This four-band view drives the AudioReactivity widget's named tile strip and the BPM strip below it. Authors who want raw eight-band resolution read chroma_AudioFFT directly in their GLSL.

docs.title: How the operator HUD uses live audio
docs.text:
Three visualizer widgets in the operator HUD read live audio over the IPC bridge:

  • AudioReactivity — Four named band tiles plus a tempo strip derived from bpm. The widget falls back to a synthetic time-domain function during the no-snapshot startup window so the UI is never blank.
  • BpmRing — Circular tempo indicator phase-locked to bpm. The ring's animation cadence reads the current snapshot directly; the synthetic fallback uses a fixed 120 BPM.
  • BeatDots — Discrete beat-pulse indicator that lights up on each beat boundary derived from bpm. The synthetic fallback fires at the same fixed tempo.

All three widgets implement a "live snapshot present" gate: when the last received snapshot is fresh, visuals run from real data; when the snapshot is stale or absent, the synthetic fallback paints. This dual mode is what lets the widgets ship as wireframe-faithful chrome before the live engine wiring lands and continue to work after the audio input source is silent.

The 48-bar FFT visualizer inside AudioReactivity and the inline 64-bar Spectrum surface in the Audio Uniforms view both stay synthetic-driven in the V1 release; live-driven retrofits are post-MVP UX work.

docs.title: Worked example: a radial pulse shader
docs.text:
A minimal scene that pulses on the bass band:

uniform float chroma_AudioFFT[8];
uniform float chroma_AudioRMS;
uniform vec2  iResolution;

void main() {
    vec2 uv  = (gl_FragCoord.xy - 0.5 * iResolution) / iResolution.y;
    float r  = length(uv);

    // Bass = bands 0 and 1 averaged.
    float bass  = 0.5 * (chroma_AudioFFT[0] + chroma_AudioFFT[1]);

    // Pulse: an inverse-distance ring that thickens with bass energy
    // and brightens with overall RMS.
    float pulse = smoothstep(0.40 - 0.20 * bass, 0.42, r)
                * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.42, 0.44 + 0.10 * bass, r));

    gl_FragColor = vec4(vec3(pulse * (0.5 + chroma_AudioRMS)), 1.0);
}

The same scene becomes a tempo-locked breathing pulse by mixing in syn_BPMSin against the radius. Authors can compose any of the audio uniforms; the binding adapter publishes them all in a stable per-pass order so per-pass uniform-buffer slot indices stay stable across reloads.

docs.title: Setting the audio threshold
docs.text:
The audio noise-floor gate is exposed as the syn_Threshold uniform and is operator-controllable through the audio settings panel and the OSC routes:

  • Shift+T samples the current 200 ms rolling RMS of syn_Level and sets the threshold to that value (also reachable as /audio/threshold/sample).
  • /audio/threshold {float} accepts an absolute threshold in [0, 1].

Audio hops with RMS below the threshold publish zeroed syn_Level* and syn_*Hits family uniforms. The threshold is the operator's primary tool for rejecting room noise, HVAC bleed, and crowd murmur in quiet sections of a show.

Authored from engine/audio/src/runtime.rs (producer thread shape), engine/audio/src/uniforms.rs (snapshot field semantics), engine/render/src/audio_adapter.rs (uniform binding contract), and the docs/adr/ADR-019-audio-uniform-ipc-bridge.md IPC contract combined with the docs/adr/ADR-006-thread-and-process-model.md thread-affinity invariants. Clean-room per docs/29-cleanroom-legal-policy-baseline.md.

docs.title: Chromaticity Uniform Reference
docs.text:
Chromaticity exposes two uniform namespaces to scene authors:

  • syn_* — the Synesthesia compatibility namespace (compat-syn-v1). These names exist for parity with reference scenes and are the primary surface authors should reach for when writing scenes that need to load on both runtimes.
  • chroma_* — the chromaticity-native namespace (native-chroma-v1). These names cover net-new analysis primitives and chromaticity-first surfaces that have no equivalent in the compatibility catalog.

Authors may mix the two namespaces freely inside a single scene. The binding adapter publishes the uniforms in a stable per-pass order; GLSL authors declare each uniform with its canonical name and type.

docs.title: Audio uniforms
docs.text: The audio analysis pipeline produces a per-tick AudioUniformSnapshot on the audio-analysis thread, which the audio-to-render adapter marshals into the GPU uniform slots below. The slice-1 producer is pure-data; the slice-2 BPM estimator carries a history-window median-smoother for tempo-following. Uniforms that read zero are the documented all-zero baseline for "no audio observed yet"; in production, the BPM uniform clamps to the default tempo (120 BPM) on the first tick before any analysis history accumulates.

docs.title: Scalar audio uniforms
docs.text: Uniform Type Range Description syn_BPM float [50, 220] Estimated tempo, clamped to the musical range syn_BPMConfidence float [0, 1] Tempo-stability confidence; near 1 when the estimator agrees across the history window syn_BPMTwitcher float [0, inf) Exponential "jump" clock; floor is the beat count, fract is the per-beat twitch syn_BPMSin float [0, 1] Sine wave at BPM frequency, beat-phase-locked syn_BPMSin2 float [0, 1] Sine wave at BPM divided by 2 syn_BPMSin4 float [0, 1] Sine wave at BPM divided by 4 syn_BPMTri float [0, 1] Triangle wave at BPM frequency syn_BPMTri2 float [0, 1] Triangle wave at BPM divided by 2 syn_BPMTri4 float [0, 1] Triangle wave at BPM divided by 4 syn_InputLevel float [0, inf) Pre-AGC instantaneous input level, computed as clamp(RMS / AGC_target, 0, inf) syn_RawLevel float [0, inf) Alias of syn_InputLevel with identical semantics syn_Threshold float [0, 1] Operator-settable noise-floor gate; audio hops below this value publish zeroed syn_Level* and syn_*Hits chroma_AudioRMS float [0, 1] Instantaneous root-mean-square energy of the mono-mixed audio frame chroma_AudioPeak float [0, 1] Instantaneous peak magnitude of the mono-mixed audio frame

docs.title: Array audio uniforms
Sampler audio uniforms
docs.text:
Uniform Type Channels Description syn_Spectrum sampler1D r=Raw FFT, g=Juiced, b=Smooth, a=Waveform Per-frame audio sampler with packed analysis variants syn_LevelTrail sampler1D r=Whole, g=Bass, b=Mid, a=High Per-band historical levels over time, newest sample at u=0

The eight-band split that chroma_AudioFFT[8] exposes is a separate surface from syn_Spectrum; the sampler retains parity with the compatibility catalog while the fixed-size array gives shader authors ergonomic indexing without a sampler lookup.

docs.title: Time uniforms
docs.text: Uniform Type Description syn_Time float Wallclock seconds since scene start syn_BassTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on bass-band hits syn_MidTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on mid-band hits syn_MidHighTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on mid-high-band hits syn_HighTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on high-band hits syn_CurvedTime float Same base as syn_Time with exponential acceleration on volume rises

docs.title: Authoring conventions
docs.text:
When a scene needs both raw analysis (the chroma_* audio primitives) and the smoothed / normalized parity surface (syn_Level*, syn_Spectrum), declare both uniforms; the binding adapter keeps the raw and smoothed paths independent so authors can pick the surface that matches each visual element. Avoid coining new syn_* names for chromaticity-native features — the Synesthesia namespace is reserved for compatibility coverage; net-new primitives belong under chroma_*.

The published GLSL spelling for every uniform on this page is exactly the canonical name; the runtime does not perform per-binding casing fixups. A typo at the GLSL declaration site silently leaves the uniform unbound, which surfaces as a warning at scene load and as a zero-valued sample at render time.

Authored from engine/render/src/audio_adapter.rs (canonical UNIFORM_NAME_* constants), engine/audio/src/uniforms.rs (producer shape and band semantics), docs/36-reactive-symbol-catalog.md (reactive symbol catalog), and the docs/adr/ADR-019-audio-uniform-ipc-bridge.md IPC contract. Clean-room per docs/29-cleanroom-legal-policy-baseline.md.

docs.title: Hotkey Reference
docs.text:
Chromaticity ships a fixed operator hotkey vocabulary covering scene and playlist transport, Snap-slot recall and capture, render and display control, the meta colour pipeline, audio threshold management, diagnostics, and show-state actions. Press ? at any time to toggle the in-app overlay that lists the same vocabulary against the active focus context.

The V1 hotkey map is read-only. Rebinding ships in V2 per the operator hotkey-map spec. The cap column on each row indicates whether the action is a free MVP capability or whether it requires an entitlement to fire; entitlement-gated rows fail closed when the matching capability is absent.

docs.title: Control-focused mode
docs.text:
Active only while a single control has keyboard focus. Esc exits control-focused mode.

Key Action D Set control to its default value R Set control to a random value in its range P Set control to its value in the current preset L Toggle the control's lock state (ignore randomization)

docs.title: Scene and playlist transport
docs.text: Key Action OSC cap Space Toggle playlist play/pause /playlist/toggleplay free ->, K Next scene in playlist /playlist/next free <-, J Previous scene in playlist /playlist/previous free Alt+Cmd+->, Ctrl+Alt+-> Jump to last in playlist /playlists/position -1 free Alt+Cmd+<-, Ctrl+Alt+<- Jump to first in playlist /playlists/position 0 free Enter Launch selected scene from the library /scenes/{name} free Shift+Enter Launch selected scene with preset prompt /scenes/{name} {preset} free Cmd+Enter, Ctrl+Enter Launch selected scene into a playlist slot (internal) free

docs.title: Snap slots
docs.text:
Per-scene quick-recall preset slots. The wire literal favslot is retained under compat-syn-v1 for OSC compatibility; the operator surface uses the name "Snap".

Key Action OSC cap 1 to 9, 0 Recall Snap slot 1 to 10 for the current scene /favslots/{n} (apply) free Shift+1 to Shift+0 Save current state to Snap slot 1 to 10 (overwrite without prompt) /favslots/{n}/save free Alt+Shift+1 to Alt+Shift+0 Clear Snap slot 1 to 10 (confirmation prompt) /favslots/{n}/clear free Cmd+S, Ctrl+S Save current state to the next empty Snap slot /favslots/{auto}/save free Cmd+Opt+S, Ctrl+Alt+S Save as a new named preset (prompts for name) /presets/new {name} free Cmd+0, Ctrl+0 Recall the scene's "gold" preset (Snap 0) /favslots/0 (apply) free

docs.title: Display and output
docs.text: Key Action cap F Toggle fullscreen on the primary output free Shift+F Toggle fullscreen on the secondary output (multi-display) free Cmd+Shift+F, Ctrl+Shift+F Cycle output window placement across displays free Cmd+\, Ctrl+\ Swap primary and secondary output free

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
Cmd+0 is globally bound to Snap 0; the former "reset resolution" binding has moved to Cmd+9.

Key Action OSC cap . Toggle render loop on/off /render/enabled {0|1} free , Toggle render-preview window (internal) free Cmd+=, Ctrl+= Step render resolution up /render/resolution {w} {h} render.custom-resolution Cmd+-, Ctrl+- Step render resolution down /render/resolution {w} {h} render.custom-resolution Cmd+9, Ctrl+9 Reset render resolution to scene default /render/resolution {sceneW} {sceneH} render.custom-resolution Cmd+Shift+=, Ctrl+Shift+= Open FPS target dialog /render/fps {float} free

docs.title: Meta controls
docs.text:
Each row enters a modal slider-adjust mode (arrow keys or scroll wheel). Esc exits the modal. The glsl column names the meta-colour uniform the binding maps onto.

Key Action glsl M Master _Master B Brightness _Brightness G Gamma _Gamma C Contrast _Contrast H Hue _Hue Y Saturation _Saturation I Invert toggle (no modal; binary flip) _Invert V Vertical mirror toggle _Vert_Mirror Shift+V Horizontal mirror toggle _Hor_Mirror E Dichrome toggle (from "Edition") _Limit_Colors

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Key Action OSC cap A Toggle audio-input mute (internal) free Cmd+A, Ctrl+A Open audio settings panel (internal) free T Toggle audio-threshold visualizer overlay (internal) free Shift+T Set audio threshold to current RMS level /audio/threshold/sample free

docs.title: Navigation panels
docs.text: Key Action Cmd+K, Ctrl+K Open command palette (searches scenes, presets, settings, help) Cmd+/, Ctrl+/ Open help and docs search Cmd+L, Ctrl+L Open scene library Cmd+,, Ctrl+, Open settings Cmd+O, Ctrl+O Open OSC and MIDI mapping panel

docs.text: Key Action Alt+Cmd+D, Ctrl+Alt+D Toggle diagnostics console Alt+Cmd+P, Ctrl+Alt+P Toggle performance HUD Alt+Cmd+L, Ctrl+Alt+L Toggle OSC and MIDI learn indicator Cmd+R, Ctrl+R Reload current scene Alt+Cmd+R, Ctrl+Alt+R Reset meta controls to defaults

docs.text:
Key Action Cmd+Shift+N, Ctrl+Shift+N New show (confirmation if unsaved changes) Cmd+Shift+O, Ctrl+Shift+O Open .chromaShow bundle Cmd+Shift+S, Ctrl+Shift+S Save show as .chromaShow bundle Cmd+Z, Ctrl+Z Undo (operator-level; one level for preset recall, meta tweak, scene switch) Cmd+Shift+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z Redo

Authored from src/lib/data/hotkeys.ts (canonical 57-row chromaticity hotkey vocabulary, mirrored from the upstream docs/42-operator-hotkey-map.md spec). Clean-room per docs/29-cleanroom-legal-policy-baseline.md.

docs.title: Importing Shadertoy Scenes
docs.text: Chromaticity ships a one-way Shadertoy-to-.chroma converter that lets authors port single-pass Shadertoy fragments directly into the Chromaticity authoring environment. The converter wraps the Shadertoy body in a chromaticity-native shell, declares the canonical Shadertoy uniforms so the body code compiles unchanged, and emits a .chroma package that the runtime then loads through the standard scene pipeline.

docs.title: What the converter accepts
docs.text:
The input is a Shadertoy GLSL body containing:

void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord) {
    // body
}

The converter wraps the body in a void main() entry that targets the naga GLSL frontend used by the engine's render path. The wrapper preamble declares the canonical Shadertoy-spelled uniforms so the imported body compiles without edits:

Uniform Purpose iTime Seconds since scene start iResolution Pixel size of the render target iTimeDelta Seconds since the previous frame iFrame Frame counter iMouse Mouse position and click state, Shadertoy-compatible

The runtime binding from these Shadertoy spellings to the canonical chromaticity-native reactive symbols (TIME, RENDERSIZE, …) is a binding-layer concern — the imported scene works in place without edits, and authors can migrate to the chromaticity-native symbols later if they want.

docs.title: What the converter rejects or warns on
docs.text:
The converter is strict about features it cannot represent in a single-pass mainImage shape. The rejection and warning surface is tagged with author-readable diagnostics:

  • VR mode (mainVR) — rejected; no plausible auto-mapping into a single-pass mainImage.
  • Cubemap entrypoint (mainCubemap) — surfaced as Warning::CubemapEntrypointDeferred; deferred to a future multipass-import pathway.
  • Webcam iChannel mapping — surfaced as Warning::WebcamIChannelDeferred; Chromaticity defers webcam binding to post-MVP. The body still compiles; the author can edit the .chroma package post-import to add a real binding.
  • Deprecated texture2D(...) calls — auto-corrected to texture(...) and surfaced as Warning::DeprecatedTexture2DAutoCorrected so the author has a trail of every machine-applied edit.

The converter is atomic: the caller sees either a fully-populated <scene_id>.chroma package or no package at all. Cleanup errors from a partially-written package are swallowed so the originating I/O cause stays surfaced in the diagnostics console.

docs.title: iChannel asset binding
docs.text:
Shadertoy scenes reference up to four iChannel0..iChannel3 slots backed by textures, cubemaps, video, audio, or the camera. The converter accepts a per-channel mapping at import time; each declared mapping causes the wrapper preamble to add a chromaticity-native binding-slot uniform (chroma_input_<channel>) and to rewrite the body's iChannelN references to that slot symbol before naga sees the source. Channels referenced by the body but not mapped at import emit Warning::MissingIChannelMapping so the author can either add the mapping in the converter and re-run, or edit the .chroma package post-import to bind the slot.

The shadertoy-fixtures/ subdirectory under <AppBundle>/Resources/scenes/ ships the iChannel asset corpus the import tests draw from — see Library Workflow for how that subdirectory is excluded from the launchable scene set.

docs.title: After import
docs.text: The output is a .chroma package matching the same on-disk shape that the in-app scaffolder produces. Once written, the package surfaces in the library through the standard discovery path and is loadable through the standard scene pipeline described in Scene Workflow. Imported scenes carry the format tag shadertoy-v1-import so the operator can filter them in the library browser.

docs.title: What is not imported
docs.text:
The Shadertoy import path is intentionally narrow:

  • ISF scenes — imported through a separate ISF-import path that is currently a reject-with-diagnostic surface; native ISF execution is deferred to V2.
  • Multi-buffer Shadertoy compositions — out of scope for the V1 import; the multipass-import pathway is a future-wave ADR.
  • Sound shaders — Chromaticity is a visual runtime; Shadertoy sound-shader bodies are rejected.

docs.title: Capability gating
docs.text: Shadertoy import is gated by the authoring.import capability. With no entitlement token present, the import action is disabled in the operator HUD with the standard locked-row affordance; see Settings Reference for the entitlement model.

docs.title: Library Workflow
docs.text: The Chromaticity library is the operator's home for browsing, searching, and launching scenes. It indexes scenes from three disjoint sources and presents them through one logical browser.

docs.title: Scene sources
docs.text:
The library merges three sources into a single result set:

  • Bundled scenes — read-only packages shipped inside the application bundle under <AppBundle>/Resources/scenes/.
  • User scenes — scenes under the active user-data scenes folder (<UserDataRoot>/Scenes/). Operators may register additional folders through Settings; results merge into the same logical library.
  • Author workspace — scenes currently open in the in-app authoring environment.

docs.title: Bundled scenes — the four-subdirectory taxonomy
docs.text:
The bundled scene root is exactly the four subdirectories named below. Discovery never walks any other path under the bundle's Resources/:

Subdirectory Purpose welcome/ Single-package first-launch onboarding scene library/ Full Chromaticity-original clean-room corpus examples/ Minimal demonstration scenes for each authoring feature (multi-pass, script, transitions, media, audio-reactive) shadertoy-fixtures/ iChannel asset fixtures consumed by Shadertoy import — not user-launchable scenes

The shadertoy-fixtures/ subdirectory is intentionally excluded from the launcher; its contents back the import path described in Scene Workflow.

docs.title: Per-scene metadata
docs.text:
Each scene exposes the following metadata to the library browser, drawn from scene.json and the package's filesystem state:

  • TITLE — display name; falls back to the package directory name when absent.
  • CREDIT — author attribution.
  • DESCRIPTION — short prose summary, surfaced in the detail pane.
  • IMAGE_PATH — relative path to the canonical thumbnail; see the thumbnail-fallback chain below.
  • TAGS and legacy CATEGORIES — searchable / filterable token lists.
  • Package path, last-modified time, scene-format tag.

The format tag is one of native-chroma-scene, compat-syn-scene, shadertoy-v1-import, or isf-import. Format tags are catalog-only — they are distinct from the runtime compatibility profile each scene also carries (compat-syn-v1 or native-chroma-v1).

docs.title: Thumbnails
docs.text:
When a scene declares an explicit IMAGE_PATH, the library loads it directly. Otherwise the loader walks a deterministic fallback chain:

  1. <package>/<package_stem>.png (matching the package directory name).
  2. An auto-generated preview captured at frame 60 with default audio-silent state.
  3. A format-family fallback icon shipped under <AppBundle>/Resources/thumbnails/ — one per scene-format tag.

Thumbnails regenerate on operator request through the scene context menu and are captured with a deterministic seeded RNG so re-renders match across runs.

docs.title: Browser capabilities
docs.text:
The library view supports both grid and list presentation. From either:

  • Full-text search across TITLE, CREDIT, DESCRIPTION, TAGS, and CATEGORIES.
  • Filter by compat profile, by tag, by presence of script.js, by presence of bundled media.
  • Sort by title, credit, last-modified, tag relevance, or author-defined order.
  • Drag a scene into the playlist editor from any view.
  • Keyboard navigation — arrow keys move the selection, Enter launches the selected scene, Shift+Enter launches with a preset prompt. See Hotkey Reference for the full vocabulary.

docs.title: Launching a scene
docs.text:
Single-click selects a scene; double-click or Enter launches it. The launch target depends on the active transport mode:

  • In playlist mode, launching a scene replaces the active playlist slot and follows the slot's transition descriptor.
  • In instant-scene mode, launching cuts directly to the scene with the operator's chosen transition.

Optional preset launch (Shift+Enter) prompts for a Snap-slot name; the default Snap is slot zero ("gold preset"). Snap slots are the operator-facing name for per-scene quick-recall presets — see the Hotkey Reference for the keyboard mappings and OSC Routes for the wire-level surface (where the literal favslots is retained for compat-syn-v1 compatibility).

docs.title: Indexing posture
docs.text: Library discovery is filesystem-backed. The indexer rescans on operator request and on filesystem-change events; for large user-scene folders, the rescan is incremental against the cached prior index. The search and filter surface in the operator HUD reads from this index over in-process IPC, not from a re-walk of disk on every keystroke.

docs.title: OSC Route Reference
docs.text: Chromaticity exposes Open Sound Control (OSC) inbound and outbound routes for show-control automation and external surface integration. This page enumerates the canonical route taxonomy honoured by the OSC adapter at the top-level prefixes the slice-2 route schema declares.

docs.title: Defaults and discovery
docs.text:
By default the OSC adapter binds the inbound listener to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) and treats the outbound target as loopback until the operator configures a routable address. Exposing the inbound listener on a routable interface is an explicit operator opt-in. The operator can confirm the bound interface and current rate-limit posture through the AdapterPill chrome at the top of any view.

Two payload-hardening defaults are pinned by the network adapter:

  • The maximum accepted OSC packet size is 64 KiB. Oversize packets are rejected with an osc-malformed-class diagnostic and no state mutation.
  • The maximum nested OSC bundle depth is 4. Deeper payloads are rejected for the same reason.

Per-route inbound traffic is rate-limited at a default ceiling of 100 messages per second per (adapter, route) pair. Over-rate messages are dropped with an osc-rate-limited diagnostic emitted no more than once per second per route to prevent the diagnostics channel itself from saturating.

docs.title: Top-level prefixes
docs.text:
The slice-2 route schema declares four canonical top-level prefixes; addresses outside this set are rejected at parse time.

Prefix Purpose /controls Scene-author parameter control (control-bank reads and writes) /scenes Scene-selection and scene-launch routes /audio Audio-pipeline routes (threshold, level discovery) /render Render-loop and resolution control

Companion route families used by the operator hotkey vocabulary (/playlist, /playlists, /favslots, /presets) are part of the broader IO surface specified in the integrations document; see the plurality and alias rules below.

docs.title: Scene routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /scenes outbound (list payload) Library scene-name listing emitted on bind and on library-change /scenes/{name} {preset?} inbound scene name; optional preset name Launch scene; unsupplied preset resolves to Snap 0 / gold /scenes/{name} outbound scene name Scene-change announcement emitted on every cut or transition completion

The legacy singular-root forms /scene/{name} and /scene/{name} {preset} are accepted as compat-syn-v1 aliases. Outbound emission during the dual-emit window publishes both the canonical plural form and the singular alias.

docs.title: Snap (favslots) routes
docs.text:
Snap is the operator-facing name for per-scene quick-recall slots; the wire-level literal favslots is retained under compat-syn-v1 for compatibility.

Route Direction Args Description /favslots/{n} inbound (apply) slot index n in [0, 15] Recall Snap slot n for the current scene /favslots/{n}/save inbound (save) slot index n Overwrite Snap slot n with the current state /favslots/{n}/clear inbound (clear) slot index n Delete Snap slot n; the slot returns to unbound /favslots/{n}/name {string} outbound slot index, name string Snap-slot name announcement on show load and after any save or clear

The apply / save / clear distinction is wire-level explicit through the route suffix; there is no implicit mode selection from message arguments. The legacy /favslots/{n} {mode} form with a string argument of "apply", "save", or "clear" is accepted as a compat-syn-v1 alias.

docs.title: Playlist routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /playlists outbound (list payload) Show-playlist listing on bind /playlists/next inbound (none) Advance to next scene in playlist /playlists/previous inbound (none) Step back to previous scene in playlist /playlists/position {i} inbound integer index; negative counts from end Jump to absolute playlist position /playlists/play inbound (none) Resume playlist transport /playlists/toggleplay inbound (none) Toggle playlist play / pause /playlists/select {name} inbound playlist name Select a named playlist as the active one /playlists/current {name} outbound active playlist name Emitted on playlist change /playlists/position {i} outbound current position Emitted on every position change

The singular-root action forms /playlist/next, /playlist/previous, /playlist/toggleplay are accepted as compat-syn-v1 aliases for the plural-root canonical forms. The hotkey overlay surfaces these singular forms in its OSC column for compatibility with reference scenes.

docs.title: Render routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /render/enabled {0|1} inbound flag Toggle the render loop on or off; the GPU scheduler halts scene rendering while UI and adapter threads stay responsive /render/resolution {w} {h} inbound width, height Resize the render output surface (capability-gated render.custom-resolution) /render/fps {float} inbound target FPS Override the render FPS target

/render/enabled 0 is non-destructive: outbound audio, MIDI, and OSC state continue to publish, and shader pipelines remain warm so the restoration frame on /render/enabled 1 is within one frame budget. Useful for SMPTE-slaved setups, A/V calibration, and operator-triggered "hold current output" cues.

docs.title: Audio routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /audio/threshold {float} inbound and outbound clamped to [0, 1] Set or announce the audio noise-floor gate; updates syn_Threshold within one audio hop /audio/threshold/sample inbound (none) Sample the current 200 ms rolling RMS of syn_Level and set the threshold to that value; emits /audio/threshold {float} outbound on completion

Audio hops with RMS below the threshold publish zeroed syn_Level* and syn_*Hits family uniforms; the threshold is the operator's primary tool for rejecting room noise and HVAC bleed.

docs.title: Controls routes
docs.text: The /controls namespace is the runtime parameter-write surface used by external surfaces (TouchOSC, MIDI-to-OSC bridges, custom show runners). The canonical shape is /controls/{bank}/{control} followed by a typed value argument; the slice-2 router parses these into a canonical segment vector for the slice-3 dispatch surface that lands the typed-command translation. Author-side scenes declare their expected control bank in the scene script; the runtime rejects writes to unknown banks with a route-mismatch diagnostic.

docs.title: Plurality convention
docs.text:
The collection roots use the plural form (/scenes, /presets, /playlists, /favslots, /controls); action verbs and listing queries live under the collection root. Chromaticity V1 canonical form is plural-root throughout inbound and outbound emission. The singular reference-app forms (/scene/{name}, /preset/{name}, /playlist/next) are accepted as compat-syn-v1 aliases.

Authored from integrations/osc-adapter/src/routes.rs (slice-2 route-prefix taxonomy) and integrations/osc-adapter/src/defaults.rs (network defaults), against docs/adr/ADR-013-networking-defaults-and-security.md and the docs/08-io-integrations.md OSC sections. Clean-room per docs/29-cleanroom-legal-policy-baseline.md.

docs.title: Perform Mode
docs.text: Perform mode is the operator's main runtime surface during a show. It arranges live scene controls, the meta colour pipeline, the media strip, the preview hero, the audio-reactivity panel, and the scene rail into a single dense layout that is reachable without opening nested panels.

docs.title: The five panels
docs.text:
The Perform view is laid out across three columns:

Column Panels Left Scene Controls, Meta Controls, Media Strip Middle Preview hero, Audio Reactivity panel Right Scene rail with Perform / Edit toggle, Setlist selector, Prev / Next / Shuffle row, scrollable scene list

Every interactive element on the surface is reachable through both mouse and keyboard.

docs.title: Scene Controls
docs.text:
The Scene Controls panel surfaces every author-declared control for the currently active scene as a typed widget — sliders for numeric parameters, toggles for booleans, swatches for colours, and combo selectors for enumerations. Each control row carries a per-control hotkey-hint badge; while a control has keyboard focus, the control-focused hotkeys take effect:

Key Action D Set the focused control to its default value R Set the focused control to a random value in its range P Set the focused control to its value in the active preset L Toggle the lock state (the locked control ignores randomisation)

The full operator hotkey vocabulary lives at Hotkey Reference.

docs.title: Meta Controls
docs.text: The Meta Controls panel exposes the scene-agnostic colour pipeline: master, brightness, gamma, contrast, hue, saturation, invert, vertical mirror, horizontal mirror, dichrome. Each meta control binds onto a canonical _Meta* uniform that is published to every scene; authors do not opt in or out of the pipeline. The hotkeys M / B / G / C / H / Y enter modal slider-adjust mode against the matching meta control; Esc exits.

docs.title: The Preview hero
docs.text: The Preview hero shows the live render output. It mirrors the actual output surface so the operator sees exactly what the audience sees. Beneath the preview, the Audio Reactivity panel surfaces the live audio uniforms — four named band tiles, the BPM strip, and the FFT visualiser.

docs.title: The Scene rail
docs.text:
The right-column scene rail surfaces:

  • A four-button rail to switch between Scenes / Presets / Edit / Add modes.
  • A Perform / Edit toggle that gates the Author surface (Edit mode is capability-gated by authoring.edit).
  • A Setlist selector pinning the active playlist.
  • A Prev / Next / Shuffle row mirroring the playlist transport hotkeys (<- / -> / Space).
  • A scrollable list of every scene in the active setlist, with the current scene highlighted.

docs.title: The Snap bar
docs.text:
A Snap bar persists across the bottom of Perform mode: ten quick-recall slots, addressed by 1 through 0 in operator focus. Saving uses Shift+1 through Shift+0; clearing uses Alt+Shift+1 through Alt+Shift+0. Slot zero is the "gold preset" and is recallable through Cmd+0 / Ctrl+0 as a guaranteed safe state.

The Snap surface is the chromaticity-native naming for what the compat-syn-v1 OSC routes still call favslots — see OSC Routes for the wire-level mapping.

docs.title: Status-bar adapter pills
docs.text:
A status bar across the bottom of Perform mode renders one pill per runtime adapter — audio, OSC, MIDI, camera, Syphon (macOS only). Each pill surfaces:

  • A connectivity dot (online / degraded / offline).
  • The bound interface or device name.
  • A click target opening the per-adapter inspector.

When an adapter is degraded, a one-line banner appears at the top of the view explaining the cause and pointing at Settings → Sources for the recovery action.

docs.title: Why Perform mode is the default
docs.text: Perform mode is the surface every operator hits first because it balances density with safety: every common live action is reachable without nesting, and the destructive actions (Snap clear, scene delete) require either a confirmation prompt or a modifier. The Author and Library views are routed under their own sidebar entries for the iteration loops where density beats safety the other way around.

docs.title: Scene Workflow
docs.text: A Chromaticity scene is an on-disk package that the runtime loads, compiles, and executes. This page covers the package layout, the load lifecycle, and the live-reload behaviour authors rely on while iterating.

docs.title: Scene package layout
docs.text:
The native package extension is .chroma. A package is a plain directory; the runtime accepts both the on-disk directory form and the .chromaPack zip transport form. The directory contains a small fixed set of files:

File Required Purpose scene.json yes Schema metadata, control declarations, pass declarations main.glsl yes Fragment-shader body for the single-pass entry point script.js no Optional script-host module: setup(), update(dt), transition() glsl/*.glsl no Shared GLSL include files images/* no Bundled media samplers used by the scene data/* reserved Reserved for the post-MVP external-data ingestion surface

The reference application's .synScene packages are accepted as import input only through the one-way Shadertoy / ISF / reference-show converters — they are never executed in place. See Library Workflow for how imported packages surface in the library after conversion.

docs.title: The load lifecycle
docs.text:
When a scene loads, it transitions through a fixed lifecycle: Unloaded → Loaded → Ready → Running. The Paused, Error, and Stopped terminal states are reachable from Running. Each transition is observable through the runtime's diagnostics console.

The compile pipeline runs in this order:

  1. Parse and validate scene.json against the canonical schema.
  2. Build the canonical internal scene model (controls, passes, transitions, media bindings, script lifecycle metadata).
  3. Preprocess GLSL — apply meta-pipeline includes and helpers.
  4. Compile shader stages and resolve the pass graph.
  5. Initialise the script sandbox, register lifecycle events.
  6. Bind resource descriptors (passes, images, media slots).

The loader runs in two modes. Strict mode enforces the canonical schema and hard-fails on contract violations; this is the default for new authoring. Compatibility mode accepts legacy keys and observed outliers from the compat-syn-v1 corpus, normalises them to the canonical model, and emits warnings — this is the mode the importers target.

docs.title: Controls and passes
docs.text:
Controls are typed parameters declared in scene.json under the CONTROLS array. Every control carries a NAME, TYPE, default, and optional range. The runtime exposes each control as a uniform of the matching GLSL type and as a script-host accessor; see the Hotkey Reference for the keyboard bindings that operate on the focused control.

Passes are declared under the PASSES array. Single-pass scenes leave PASSES empty and use main.glsl directly; multipass scenes name each pass and reference earlier passes via the multipass uniforms documented under Chromaticity Uniforms.

docs.title: Live reload while authoring
docs.text:
The authoring environment watches every file in the active package and applies a per-file reload policy:

!!! note "Live-reload policy by file type"

- `scene.json` — full scene rebuild; control state preserved where
  `NAME` is unchanged across the edit.
- `main.glsl` — recompile only; control values, script state, and
  pass targets are preserved as long as pass declarations are
  unchanged.
- `glsl/*.glsl` — same as `main.glsl` for every scene currently
  using the include.
- `script.js` — rebind the script host, re-run `setup()`, keep
  control values, reset script-local state.
- `images/*` — reload the affected sampler; everything else is
  preserved.

The shader-edit-to-visible-result latency budget is p95 ≤ 500 ms on the MVP hardware class. Hot reloads are not allowed to drop output frames; if a recompile exceeds the frame budget, the new shader is swapped in on the next frame boundary.

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text: Each scene declares its accepted transition shapes through the HARD_TRANSITIONS and SMOOTH_TRANSITIONS keys. Transition triggers are tied to runtime transition events (manual cuts, audio-driven cues, playlist advancement). Transition variables are projected into scene uniforms before pass execution so authors can sample them in GLSL or JavaScript.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
The authoring console streams diagnostics from every subsystem (GLSL compiler, JS host, OSC and MIDI adapters, audio adapter, media adapter) tagged with timestamp, subsystem, scene name, and severity. The coerce severity covers every compatibility-mode coercion the loader applies — useful when porting reference scenes to the canonical model.

GLSL compile errors map back to the author's source line through a post-prepend mapping table, so the meta-pipeline header injected at compile time does not skew line numbers. JSON schema violations link directly to the offending path.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text: Settings is where operators bring up the audio device, configure the output pipeline, register storage paths, and review the entitlement surface. The view is laid out as four operator-bring-up sections at the top, followed by the General toggles, the Hotkeys reference, and the Theme switcher.

docs.title: 1. Audio Device
docs.text:
The Audio Device section enumerates host audio devices through the audio adapter's input and output pickers. The fields surfaced are:

  • Input device — the microphone or capture interface feeding the analysis pipeline.
  • Output device — the playback target the runtime mixes to.
  • Sample rate — typically 48 kHz on macOS, 44.1 kHz on Windows consumer hardware.
  • Latency hint — low, balanced, or high. Lower hints reduce the wallclock between an audio event and its visual response, at the cost of buffer-underrun risk under CPU pressure.
  • Channel layout — the input channel mapping used by the mono mix-down.
  • Input gain — pre-AGC trim in dB.
  • Live level / peak meter — confirms the chosen device is producing signal before scene launch.

Changes apply at the next analysis-thread restart (typically the next scene load); the analysis thread does not hot-swap audio devices mid-show to keep the snapshot pipeline deterministic.

docs.title: 2. Graphics and Output
docs.text:
The Graphics section covers everything between the renderer and the display:

  • Resolution — preset list (1080p, 1440p, 4K, …) plus a custom width × height entry. The custom entry is gated by the render.custom-resolution capability.
  • Render scale — fractional under-sample for performance-budget bring-up; defaults to 1.0.
  • Target FPS — the render-loop ceiling. Lower targets free GPU headroom for heavy multipass scenes.
  • V-Sync — when enabled, the present pacing is tied to the display's refresh; when disabled, the renderer free-runs at the FPS target.
  • HDR target — capability-gated; reserved for V2 hardware that exposes a 10-bit HDR swap chain.
  • Display assignment — selects which physical display the output window paints to in multi-display setups.

docs.title: 3. Storage
docs.text:
The Storage section pins the filesystem locations the runtime reads and writes:

  • Media folders — directories searched for IMAGE_PATH, video samplers, and the per-scene images/ symlink targets.
  • Custom scene folders — extra directories merged into the library results alongside <UserDataRoot>/Scenes/. See Library Workflow for how merging works.
  • Backups path — destination for crash-restore snapshots and show-bundle exports, with a configurable retention window.
  • Cache cleanup — buttons to clear the thumbnail cache and the shader-compile cache. Useful when a scene authoring round-trip has poisoned a cached artifact.

Each path field has a Browse button that invokes the native folder-picker through the shell IPC layer.

docs.title: 4. Network and adapter defaults
docs.text:
Chromaticity ships network-conservative by default — every adapter binds to loopback unless the operator explicitly opts in. The defaults matter because OSC and NDI carry no built-in authentication:

Adapter Default bind Opt-in path OSC inbound 127.0.0.1 (loopback) Operator selects an interface or 0.0.0.0 OSC outbound 127.0.0.1 target Operator sets per-subscriber target IP NDI input local subnet discovery Operator restricts to allowlist NDI output local subnet advertise Operator sets local-host-only or denylist Syphon and Spout local-host only n/a (protocol constraint)

Per-mapping source-IP allowlists honour CIDR notation (192.168.1.0/24) so a venue-Wi-Fi setup can trust a single subnet without opening every interface. Inbound traffic is rate-limited at 1000 messages per second per adapter (hard cap) and 100 messages per second per (adapter, route) pair (operator-floor default).

!!! warning "Changing a network setting may expose Chromaticity to the network"

Every override on this surface carries the explicit warning above.
Overrides are persisted per show, so exporting a `.chromaShow`
bundle reproduces the operator's network posture on the
destination machine.

See OSC Routes for the route taxonomy and payload hardening defaults the OSC adapter enforces.

docs.title: 5. Entitlement and capabilities
docs.text:
Settings surfaces the active entitlement token and the resolved capability bitmask. Chromaticity's entitlement model is data-only — the runtime evaluates per-capability flags against a single in-memory EntitlementSet; there is no runtime concept of an "edition".

The following capabilities ship unconditionally free in every install, including with no token present:

  • Pause and transport control.
  • Hard-cut transitions (transitions-off).
  • Playlist navigation (next, previous, select).
  • Preset recall and Snap slots.
  • Scene export (for backup or hand-off).
  • OSC and MIDI route discovery messages.
  • Camera input (io.camera).

Capabilities that gate behind a valid token include the watermark removal (render.watermark.off), the OSC and Syphon I/O surfaces, the in-app authoring environment (authoring.ide), Shadertoy and ISF import (authoring.import), scene editing (authoring.edit), and the custom-resolution surface (render.custom-resolution).

docs.title: 6. Theme
docs.text: The Theme switcher cycles among the three shipped themes (Pulse, Atelier, Console). Themes are aesthetic options — they swap colour palettes and surface treatments without changing layout or workflow.
